text: Misplacement of the catheter has been reported.3,5 Precip- itation of minerals, lipids, and medications can cause line oc- clusion.3 Thrombophlebitis can occur after the use of either peripheral or central veins. Although it has been suggested that infusion of hyperosmolar solutions via a central line is less likely to produce thrombophlebitis, because the feed is immediately diluted by a large volume of blood, major thrombotic complications such as pulmonary embolism and right atrial thrombosis could be more common than hitherto recognised in children and adolescents re- ceiving long term parenteral nutrition via central catheters.6,7 The use of a fine-bore silicone catheter peripherally may avoid the need for central vein cannulation8 and there is a lower incidence of thrombophlebitis when fine-bore silicone catheters rather than teflon ones are used for peripheral parenteral nutrition.9 The use of giving sets with filters may decrease thrombophlebitis during peripheral infusion.10,11 The addition of heparin or buffer solu- tions to the feed, and the use of local hydrocortisone and glyceryl trinitrate, has also been reported to prolong the survival of pe- ripheral infusion sites.11,12 Extravasation may also be a problem, particularly with hyperosmolar solutions, and has led to severe tissue damage; hyaluronidase or thiomucase may be used in the treatment of such extravasation.13 Parenteral nutrition may be associated with atrophic changes in the mucosal structure and enzymic activity of the intestine, lead- Nutritional Agents and Vitamins 1925 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) ing to increased permeability with a possible increased risk of bacteraemia and endotoxaemia. These changes, which have been attributed to lack of glutamine (which is unstable in solution), can reportedly be prevented by addition of glutamine-releasing dipeptides to solutions for total parenteral nutrition—see p.1947. Some have questioned the extent of this mucosal atrophy or bac- terial translocation associated with parenteral feeding.14,15 Prolonged parenteral nutrition has been associated with hepato- biliary complications, especially in children;16,17 cholelithiasis and cholestasis have been reported, with the latter sometimes progressing to liver failure.18 Although the aetiology is consid- ered multifactorial,18 contamination of the solution with manga- nese (see Accumulation under Adverse Effects of Manganese, p.1956) or aluminium19 has been suggested as one possible cause of the cholestasis.
